## Upgrade

- **No migrations.** Replace the binaries and restart. See [Upgrading from 3.0.11 to 3.0.12](/docs/migrations#upgrading-from-3-0-11-to-3-0-12).
- **`::hot::store/put-many` and `merge` store all of their entries or none.** On 3.0.11 a call that failed part-way left the entries before the failing one.

## Fixes

- **`::hot::store/put-many` and `merge` write one batch.** They wrote each entry with its own transaction, storage admission and commit. On PostgreSQL each entry was also read by its key twice before it was written, and under row-level security a read by key goes through every entry of the store, so an import cost more the more the store held. On a deployed Hot whose PostgreSQL has one vCPU, 1,000 entries took 20 to 65 seconds with the database at 100% CPU. A batch is now one transaction. PostgreSQL writes it with one statement for every 1,000 entries and reads nothing by key. Two batches that write some of the same keys still cannot block each other for good: entries are locked in the order of their keys, and a batch that PostgreSQL ends to break a deadlock is written again. Times on PostgreSQL 18 with one CPU, as a runtime login, for the first write of the keys and then the same keys again:

  | Entries | Store already holds | 3.0.11 | 3.0.12 |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 1,000 | nothing | 2.5 s / 3.2 s | 0.09 s / 0.08 s |
  | 1,000 | 20,000 entries | 17.8 s / 16.3 s | 0.09 s / 0.08 s |
  | 10,000 | nothing | 65 s / 144 s | 1.05 s / 0.68 s |
  | 10,000 | 20,000 entries | 235 s / 238 s | 1.12 s / 0.68 s |

  On SQLite 10,000 entries go from 1.39 s to 0.20 s.
- **`::hot::store/put` on PostgreSQL** is one statement instead of two, and under row-level security no longer reads through the store before it writes. With 20,000 entries in the store a `put` took about 16 ms and now takes about 2.5 ms.
- **Reading one store entry by a string key uses an index on PostgreSQL.** `::hot::store/get`, `delete`, `put-if` and `increment` found their entry by its jsonb key, which under row-level security reads every entry of the store. For a string key they now also match the key's text, which PostgreSQL can look up. Time for one call on PostgreSQL 18 with one CPU, as a runtime login:

  | Store holds | Call | 3.0.11 | 3.0.12 |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 2,000 entries | `get` | 1.6 ms | 0.27 ms |
  | 20,000 entries | `get` | 11.4 ms | 0.34 ms |
  | 20,000 entries | `increment` | 22.8 ms | 1.8 ms |
  | 20,000 entries | `get` then `put-if` | 35.0 ms | 2.3 ms |
  | 20,000 entries | `delete` | 21.9 ms | 0.9 ms |

  A key that is not a string, such as a number or a vector, is still found by reading the store's entries.
- **A large store value that one batch writes and then replaces** is released from blob storage. Its blob used to stay.

## Behaviour changes

- **A `put-many` or `merge` that fails stores nothing.** The entries are one transaction, so a failure such as the account's storage limit no longer leaves the entries before it.
- **The entries of one batch share one `updated_at`.**
- **`::hot::store/put-if-missing` on an account at its storage limit** answers `false` when another writer created the key first. It could answer with the limit error.

## Dependencies

- **lettre 0.11.24** fixes six advisories in the SMTP client that sends Hot's mail (RUSTSEC-2026-0560 to RUSTSEC-2026-0565): forged replies through STARTTLS, command injection through a bare LF or CR in a message, mail for a quoted local part going to a different address, two panics on a malformed reply or display name, and unbounded buffering of a reply.
